text: You could paste Lesson 3's query straight into Power BI and call it done. It would even work, once. But every week, when the scheduled refresh runs, Power BI would re-run that exact literal text with no single place to review or fix the logic if a business rule changes. A view fixes that: one object, living in the database, testable on its own.

The fact view carries keys only, exactly per the Lesson 2 architecture: SalesOrderID, OrderDate, DueDate, ShipDate, TerritoryID, ProductID, OrderQty, UnitPrice, LineTotal. Filtered to Status equals 5, Shipped. No TerritoryName, no ProductName. Those live in two small dimension views: ProductDim, with a LEFT JOIN to subcategory so products without one still get a row, and TerritoryDim, a straight pass-through of SalesTerritory.

Notice CREATE OR ALTER VIEW, not just CREATE VIEW. That lets you re-run this script safely while iterating, instead of erroring out because the object already exists. That matters specifically because Lesson 15's change request comes back to modify this exact fact view again.

After creating all three views, run a COUNT on the fact view and compare it to the number you verified back in Lesson 2 and Lesson 3. It should match exactly. If it doesn't, the view's join or filter doesn't match what you already confirmed, and that's worth fixing right here, before Power BI ever sees it.

Three staged views now sit in AdventureWorks2012, ready to be read like ordinary tables. Next lesson: bringing all three into Power BI and building the actual data model, with real relationships between them.
